Uber's deal to put 2,000 Pony.ai robotaxis on European roads, BYD's 31-degree-of-freedom humanoid hitting showroom floors, and Unitree's disclosure that it has already shipped some 18,000 humanoid robots mark the week physical AI stopped being a lab trick and started looking like an industry.

Every carmaker, it seems, now wants to build a robot, and every ride-hailing app wants a fleet it doesn't have to own. This week's stories trace both trends at once — Honda, BYD, Hyundai and LG racing into humanoids while Uber leans harder into partnerships than proprietary tech — with drones, as usual, colonizing every remaining niche from wind turbines to mosquitoes.

Humanoid robot traffic officer patrols the streets in China

A humanoid robot has begun patrolling streets in Wuhu, China, taking on traffic enforcement duties.

Why it matters. A humanoid directing traffic in Wuhu is more theater than infrastructure for now, but it's a real public deployment, not a trade-show stunt. Watch whether Chinese municipalities treat this as a template — cheap, telegenic proof of 'smart city' progress — or quietly walk it back after the novelty fades.

Read at WPLG Local 10 →

Waymo gets regulatory approval to scale up robotaxi service across California, enter 2 new markets

Waymo

Waymo won California regulatory clearance to expand its driverless robotaxi service statewide and into two additional markets.

Read at Fox Business →

LG, NVIDIA Unveil AI-Powered Humanoid Robot

LG, NVIDIA

LG and NVIDIA unveiled an AI-powered humanoid robot, combining the appliance maker's hardware expertise with NVIDIA's computing platform.

Read at chosun.com →

Waymo Widens California Reach, Adds Sacramento to Bay Area and L.A. Rollout

Waymo

Waymo is broadening its robotaxi footprint across California, expanding service in the Bay Area and Los Angeles while also winning state regulatory approval to begin driverless operations in Sacramento. The moves push the company's driverless ambitions into a third major California market, layering new territory onto its existing Northern and Southern California operations.

Read at ABC7 Bay Area →

Self-driving trucks are officially testing on California highways

Aurora Innovation, Kodiak AI, California Department of Motor Vehicles

Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI have secured permits to test autonomous heavy-duty trucks on California highways, ending the state's prior ban on driverless vehicles over ten thousand pounds.

Read at TechCrunch →

Waymo Widens Its Map, Adding Arizona Suburbs and Sacramento

Waymo

Waymo keeps filling in the blanks on its robotaxi map: the company is rolling into Gilbert and Mesa, Arizona, though it says the West Valley isn't next in line, while in California it has secured regulatory approval to begin driverless rides in Sacramento. Together the moves push the service well beyond its original San Francisco and Los Angeles strongholds into a patchwork of new suburbs and state capitals.

Read at FOX40 →

Off Denmark, a drone flew around a wind turbine while its blades were still spinning and inspected them without forcing the machine to stop generating electricity

RWE, Quali Drone, Energy Cluster Denmark, Rødsand 2 Offshore Wind Farm, Technical University of Denmark

RWE and Danish startup Quali Drone tested an autonomous drone that inspected offshore wind turbine blades while they spun, avoiding costly shutdowns.

Why it matters. Inspecting a spinning turbine blade without stopping it sounds trivial until you price out lost generation time across an offshore wind farm. RWE and Quali Drone's test points toward drones becoming standard maintenance infrastructure for an industry that hates downtime.

Read at Energies Media →

New British Drone Tricks Enemy Radar Into Seeing a Target 20 Times Larger

British defense contractor

A British defense contractor has deployed a drone equipped with radar-deception technology that amplifies its perceived size by a factor of twenty.

Why it matters. Making a drone look twenty times its actual size to radar is cheap deception with expensive consequences for anyone trying to shoot it down. It's the kind of asymmetric trick that pressures air-defense budgets faster than it pressures drone budgets.

Read at The Defense Post →

2026 FIFA World Cup Public Safety Drone Operations

Skydio, Mira Marquez, Ryan Blinn

Skydio deployed drones for public safety operations at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, conducting over 10,000 flights.

Read at Skydio →

Over 2,000 humanoid robots to compete in Beijing games

Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology, Smart Analytics Global, Jiang Guangzhi, Beril Canakci

Over two thousand humanoid robots from sixteen countries converge in Beijing this month for competitions testing machines on soccer, martial arts, and factory work.

Read at Anadolu Ajansı →

Chinese humanoid robot maker Unitree powers up for stellar Shanghai debut

Unitree

Unitree is debuting its humanoid robot at Shanghai's trade show, staking China's claim in a global race to commercialize physical AI.

Read at Reuters →

LG Group plans humanoid robot reveal in early 2027 - report

LG Group

LG Group is planning to unveil a humanoid robot in early 2027, marking the conglomerate's entry into physical AI robotics.

Why it matters. LG waiting until 2027 to show a humanoid is a tell that the conglomerate sees itself playing catch-up to Hyundai, Samsung and the Chinese automakers already shipping hardware. The lag also hints at how much runway LG thinks it needs to make its own bet credible.

Read at Investing.com →

Unitree Robotics rolls out around 18,000 humanoid robots to date

Unitree Robotics

Unitree Robotics has deployed roughly 18,000 of its humanoid robots, marking a significant scale-up in physical AI adoption.

Why it matters. Eighteen thousand humanoids is a scale number no Western competitor has publicly matched, and it turns Unitree from a viral video subject into an actual manufacturing story. The figure will pressure rivals to disclose their own numbers or explain why they can't.

Read at Gasgoo →

Unidata Launches a Network of Data-Capture Stations for Humanoid Robots

Unidata

Unidata is deploying a network of data-capture stations designed to train and coordinate humanoid robots in real-world environments.

Why it matters. Data, not hardware, is the real bottleneck for humanoid robots, and Unidata's stations are a bet on becoming the picks-and-shovels layer for training them in messy real-world settings. Whoever controls the data pipeline could end up with more leverage than the robot makers themselves.

Read at The Des Moines Register →

Uber's Robotaxi Blitz: 2,000 Pony.ai Cars for Europe, Plus a Tokyo Push

Uber Technologies, Uber, Pony.ai, Dara Khosrowshahi

Uber is moving on two fronts at once: a deal with China's Pony.ai to deploy 2,000 robotaxis across Europe, and an expansion into Japan, where a Tokyo pilot is underway. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi called Japan a 'terrific' market for the company, framing the rollout as proof that Uber can scale autonomous rides globally by stacking partnerships rather than building its own self-driving tech. The strategy bets that sheer fleet size and geographic reach can outpace the regulatory and technical snags that have dogged robotaxi rivals.

Why it matters. Two thousand robotaxis is the largest single robotaxi commitment announced this year, and it confirms Uber's strategy of stacking third-party autonomy partners rather than building its own stack, à la Waymo. The Tokyo push adds a second front, testing whether Uber's aggregator model travels as well in Japan's tightly regulated taxi market as it has elsewhere.

Read at simplywall.st →

Waymo Partners with Las Vegas Raiders & Allegiant Stadium

Waymo, Las Vegas Raiders, Allegiant Stadium

Waymo will operate autonomous shuttles for Las Vegas Raiders fans attending events at Allegiant Stadium, expanding its ride-hailing footprint into sports venue logistics.

Read at CleanTechnica →

Anduril unveiled an armed drone gunship to fly with Apaches, and the crew it replaces was the one taking the most risk

Anduril

Anduril revealed an armed drone gunship designed to operate alongside Apache helicopters, targeting the most vulnerable crew positions in attack formations.

Why it matters. Anduril building a drone specifically to fly the riskiest slot in an Apache formation is a blunt statement about where the company thinks military manpower should — and shouldn't — be spent. It's a preview of how attack aviation gets restructured once autonomous wingmen become reliable enough to trust with the dangerous jobs.

Read at OkDiario →

Shield AI Flies Taiwan Drone Swarm Without Human Pilots

Shield AI

Shield AI deployed an autonomous drone swarm in Taiwan that operated without human pilots, demonstrating the company's advances in fully autonomous flight.

Why it matters. Flying a fully pilotless drone swarm in Taiwan is as much a geopolitical signal as a technical one, given the island's precarious position. Shield AI is effectively demonstrating a deterrent capability in public, which is unusual for a defense contractor and worth watching for how Beijing responds.

Read at Dallas Innovates →

item.title: The Weekly — 2026-W32
item.description: Boston Dynamics anchors the week with a Hyundai joint venture to commercialize Atlas, a $100M Waltham facility expansion, and its Stretch warehouse robot, while HII commits up to $900 million to Path Robotics and GrayMatter Robotics and driverless freight and robotaxis (Austin trucks, Waymo in Denver, Oro Mobility/Uber/Hertz) push autonomy further into daily commerce.
item.content:encoded:
Boston Dynamics anchors the week with a Hyundai joint venture to commercialize Atlas, a $100M Waltham facility expansion, and its Stretch warehouse robot, while HII commits up to $900 million to Path Robotics and GrayMatter Robotics and driverless freight and robotaxis (Austin trucks, Waymo in Denver, Oro Mobility/Uber/Hertz) push autonomy further into daily commerce.

This week the robots stopped auditioning and started clocking in: Boston Dynamics is building a factory to match its ambitions, HII is writing nine-figure checks for welding and finishing bots, and driverless trucks and taxis are quietly normalizing themselves on American streets from Austin to Denver. Meanwhile the drone world keeps finding new jobs for itself, from Navy resupply runs to Tokyo spectator sport.

World's largest humanoid robot maker Unitree's founder becomes billionaire ahead of IPO

Unitree, Wang Shengsheng

Unitree founder Wang Shengsheng becomes a billionaire as the world's largest humanoid robot maker prepares for its IPO.

Read at VnExpress International →

Waymo enters second phase of testing in Denver

Waymo

Waymo is expanding its autonomous-vehicle testing in Denver to a second phase of real-world operations.

Read at CBS News →

Arrive AI and LifeSpan Pharmacy Announce Letter of Intent to Explore Autonomous Drone Pharmacy Delivery Program

Arrive AI, LifeSpan Pharmacy

Arrive AI and LifeSpan Pharmacy signed a letter of intent to pilot autonomous drone delivery for pharmacy orders.

Read at finance.yahoo.com →

Ondas Selected to Provide Advanced Counter-Drone Protection for Jacksonville Jaguars NFL Games

Ondas

Ondas will deploy counter-drone technology at Jacksonville Jaguars home games, marking a commercial entry for the wireless-security company into sports-venue protection.

Why it matters. Counter-drone security is moving from military bases to Sunday football, a sign that the threat of rogue drones over crowds has become mainstream enough to warrant stadium-grade defense. Ondas' entry into sports venues opens a new commercial vertical beyond its traditional defense and critical-infrastructure customers, and other leagues will be watching whether the Jaguars deal becomes a template.

Read at Newswire.com →

Boston Dynamics Introduces Stretch: A Mobile Manipulation Robot for Logistics Automation

Boston Dynamics

Boston Dynamics unveiled Stretch, a mobile manipulation robot designed to automate warehouse loading and unloading tasks.

Why it matters. Stretch is Boston Dynamics' pivot from spectacle to spreadsheet: a robot built to solve the unglamorous but expensive problem of unloading trucks and trailers. It puts Boston Dynamics in direct competition with warehouse automation players like Fetch and Locus, betting that logistics, not backflips, pays the bills.

Read at Boston Dynamics →

Boston Dynamics and TM Robotics Partner to Bring Spot to EMEA

Boston Dynamics, TM Robotics

Boston Dynamics expands Spot's reach into Europe, the Middle East, and Africa through a partnership with distributor TM Robotics.

Read at Boston Dynamics →

Waymo's launch of robotaxis in Colorado nears. What to know

Waymo

Waymo is preparing to deploy its robotaxi service in Colorado, expanding its self-driving operations beyond California and Arizona.

Read at The Coloradoan →

Driverless freight trucks are now running through Austin

Autonomous freight operator

Autonomous freight trucks are operating in Austin, marking a milestone in the commercialization of self-driving commercial vehicles.

Why it matters. Driverless trucks running actual freight routes in Austin marks the shift from closed-course testing to public highways carrying real cargo. It puts pressure on Aurora and Kodiak's timelines and raises the stakes for how regulators and the public react once autonomous trucks become a common sight rather than a novelty.

Read at Austin American-Statesman →

Amazon's Zoox to start paid robotaxi rides in Vegas next week

Amazon, Zoox

Amazon's Zoox begins commercial robotaxi service in Las Vegas, marking the company's transition from testing to paid autonomous rides.

Read at Reuters →

DZYNE to Scale Grasshopper Resupply Drone Development for US Air Force

DZYNE

DZYNE is scaling production of its Grasshopper resupply drone for the U.S. Air Force, moving the autonomous cargo vehicle from prototype to operational deployment.

Why it matters. Scaling a resupply drone from prototype to Air Force operations is the harder, less glamorous half of defense innovation, where budgets and doctrine matter more than demos. DZYNE's progress here is a bellwether for how quickly autonomous logistics can actually enter the military supply chain versus just appearing in press releases.

Read at The Defense Post →

MicroVision Gives Drones a New Way to See in 3D

MicroVision

MicroVision has developed a 3D vision technology designed to enhance drone perception capabilities.

Why it matters. Better 3D perception is the unsexy backbone that makes every flashy drone capability actually work in cluttered, real-world environments. MicroVision's push here matters for anyone building autonomous navigation stacks, since vision quality is often the bottleneck rather than flight controls.

Read at The Defense Post →

NCSIST and Shield AI complete autonomous drone mission

NCSIST, Shield AI

NCSIST and Shield AI demonstrated an autonomous drone mission, marking progress in their partnership on unmanned systems for defense applications.

Read at digitimes →

Delivering throughout the tournament

Wing

Wing secured FAA authorization to conduct drone deliveries throughout the FIFA World Cup in Dallas and Charlotte, operating in restricted airspace during the tournament.

Read at Wing →

X10 Camera Updates Draper Release

Skydio

Skydio released camera updates to its X10 drone, improving low-light performance, autofocus reliability, and adding click-to-focus capability.

Why it matters. Incremental as it sounds, better low-light and autofocus performance is what determines whether a drone is useful at dusk or in a warehouse aisle, not just in bright daylight demos. Skydio's steady iteration on the X10 keeps it ahead of DJI-adjacent competitors in the U.S. enterprise and public-safety drone market.

Read at Skydio →

Mitsubishi joins the humanoid robot race — at a 1,000 unit per month pace

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries is manufacturing humanoid robots at 1,000 units per month, entering the commercialization race with what appears to be the industry's first volume production operation.

Read at Electrek →

'World's first embodied all-terrain' humanoid robot Lumo unveiled

Lumo

Bipedal robotics startup Lumo has revealed what it claims is the first all-terrain humanoid robot capable of traversing rough ground without wheels.

Why it matters. An all-terrain bipedal humanoid claims to solve the mobility problem that has dogged most warehouse-bound humanoids, which mostly shuffle across flat, polished floors. If Lumo's claims hold up outside a press release, it puts pressure on Figure, Apptronik and others to prove their robots can handle anything rougher than a loading dock.

Read at Interesting Engineering →

HII signs up to $900M agreement with Path Robotics, GrayMatter Robotics

HII, Path Robotics, GrayMatter Robotics

HII commits up to $900 million to deploy robots from Path Robotics and GrayMatter Robotics across its manufacturing operations.

Why it matters. Nine figures for welding and surface-finishing robots is a serious bet that shipbuilding, one of manufacturing's most labor-strapped corners, can be automated at scale. This deal is a major proof point for Path Robotics and GrayMatter, and a signal to other heavy-industry primes that robotic welding has moved past pilot projects.

Read at The Robot Report →

Robot Fighting Competition Becomes Paid Spectator Sport in Tokyo

Tokyo has commercialized robot fighting as a ticketed spectator sport, turning what was once a hobbyist niche into a revenue-generating entertainment venue.

Why it matters. Turning robot combat into a ticketed spectator sport suggests robotics culture is maturing into entertainment the way monster trucks or MMA once did, giving hobbyist engineering a commercial afterlife. It's a small but telling data point on how publicly robots are now consumed as spectacle rather than just industrial tools.

Read at 조선일보 →

item.title: The Weekly — 2026-W31
item.description: Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2 gives humanoids full-body control, Amazon's Zoox becomes the first company cleared to run paid robotaxis without a human behind the wheel, and Waymo keeps scaling hard — importing thousands of Chinese-made Geely sedans while pushing into Napa, D.C., and six new cities.
item.content:encoded:
Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2 gives humanoids full-body control, Amazon's Zoox becomes the first company cleared to run paid robotaxis without a human behind the wheel, and Waymo keeps scaling hard — importing thousands of Chinese-made Geely sedans while pushing into Napa, D.C., and six new cities.

This was the week physical AI stopped being a demo and started being logistics. Waymo and Zoox both notched real regulatory and operational milestones, DeepMind showed off a model that can move a robot's whole body instead of just its arm, and a Qualcomm humanoid reminded everyone that the stage between lab and street is still littered with faceplants.

Tau Robotics launches humanoid robot home cleaning service in San Francisco

Tau Robotics

Tau Robotics has begun deploying humanoid robots to clean homes in San Francisco, marking a commercial entry into domestic physical AI.

Read at ABC10 →

Google DeepMind says Gemini Robotics 2 enables full body control

Google DeepMind

Google DeepMind released Gemini Robotics 2, a model capable of controlling a robot's full body rather than individual limbs.

Why it matters. Most humanoid demos still stitch together scripted single-limb motions; full-body control is the harder, more useful trick, letting a robot coordinate legs, torso and arms to actually do physical work. It puts pressure on Figure, Tesla, and Unitree, who all need this kind of unified control to move past choreographed showcases.

Read at therobotreport.com →

Qualcomm-powered robot collapses spectacularly on stage during company's keynote — prepared stagehands rush to cloak and then carry off stricken humanoid (updated)

Qualcomm

A Qualcomm-powered humanoid robot failed catastrophically during the company's keynote presentation, collapsing on stage before stagehands removed it.

Read at Tom's Hardware →

100 driverless oilfield trucks planned for Permian Basin as US firms scale fleet by 2027

US oilfield operators

US oilfield operators are planning to deploy 100 autonomous trucks in the Permian Basin by 2027, marking a significant expansion of driverless vehicles into energy infrastructure.

Read at Interesting Engineering →

DoorDash launches in-house drone delivery program after FAA certification

DoorDash

DoorDash launched its own drone delivery operation after securing FAA certification, moving beyond third-party logistics partnerships.

Read at CNBC →

Amazon's steering wheel- and brake pedal-less Zoox robotaxis receive nation's first go-ahead for paid public rides

Amazon, Zoox

Amazon's Zoox has won regulatory approval to operate fully autonomous robotaxis for paying passengers in California, marking the first such clearance for a steering-wheel-free vehicle in the U.S.

Read at Planetizen →

Waymo Pushes Deeper Into California, Even as Santa Monica Cries Foul

Waymo

Waymo appears poised to go fully driverless in Sacramento within weeks, a city councilmember says, extending its robotaxi footprint further into California's interior. Meanwhile, down the coast in Santa Monica, the company is fighting a city ban on overnight charging at two of its taxi stations, arguing the restriction threatens round-the-clock service. The two fronts capture Waymo's current phase: expanding fast while haggling with cities over the mundane logistics of keeping a robot fleet powered.

Read at Sacramento Bee →

Defense drone company takes step toward Nasdaq debut

An unnamed defense drone company has filed for a Nasdaq listing, signaling consolidation in the commercial unmanned-aircraft sector.

Why it matters. A drone maker heading toward Nasdaq is a small data point in a bigger trend: defense-tech and drone companies chasing public capital as procurement budgets and Ukraine-driven demand make the sector look investable. Watch whether public markets reward these listings or treat them skeptically after a wave of SPAC-era disappointments.

Read at The Business Journals →

BYD's Humanoid Robot to Debut in August

BYD

BYD will debut its humanoid robot in August, signaling the Chinese automaker's push into physical AI manufacturing.

Read at Gasgoo →

Waymo adds 6 new cities for driverless rides, but Sacramento still waiting

Waymo

Waymo is expanding its driverless ride-hailing service to six new cities, though Sacramento—where it has faced regulatory pushback—remains excluded from the rollout.

Why it matters. Six new cities is Waymo flexing its scale advantage over every other robotaxi player. But Sacramento's continued exclusion is the more interesting story — a reminder that regulatory pushback, not technology, remains the binding constraint on how fast this expansion can actually go.

Read at The Business Journals →

Amazon (AMZN) Wins First US Approval For Zoox Driverless Robotaxi Service

Amazon, Zoox

Amazon's Zoox has received the first U.S. regulatory approval to operate a driverless robotaxi service, clearing a major hurdle for commercial autonomous vehicle deployment.

Read at simplywall.st →

Waymo Clears Bigger Path Toward Napa Valley

Waymo

Waymo expands its driverless taxi service into Napa Valley, broadening its footprint beyond the Bay Area.

Why it matters. Wine country is a different market than dense urban grids: lower density, tourist traffic, winding roads. Waymo testing there suggests the company sees demand beyond commuter rides, in leisure and tourism markets that ride-hailing incumbents haven't fully cracked with autonomy.

Read at Patch →

Autonomous AI-powered drone tech detects and reports fires, test launched by five-way partnership

Israel Aerospace Industries, Technion, Israel Innovation Authority, Fire and Rescue Authority, National Security Ministry, Yaron Shein, Eyal Caspi

Israel Aerospace Industries and four government partners launched an AI-powered drone that spots wildfires within minutes, autonomously scanning for hours.

Read at The Jerusalem Post →

New UAV Pushes Battlefield Sensing Into the Stratosphere

Icarus, US Army

Icarus is pitching the Army a solar-powered drone that can loiter above 60,000 feet and watch an area the size of Delaware with minimal latency.

Why it matters. A solar drone loitering above 60,000 feet for days at a time is a step toward persistent, cheap surveillance that doesn't rely on satellites or manned aircraft. For the Army, it's a cost-effective way to watch huge swaths of contested territory continuously — the kind of capability that changes how battlefield intelligence gets gathered.

Read at The Defense Post →

Central Asia’s first autonomous delivery system debuts in Astana

Alatau Advance Air Group, Daniyar Uteulin

Alatau Advance Air Group launched Central Asia's first autonomous drone delivery system at Astana's Games of the Future, ferrying snacks and souvenirs to smart lockers.

Why it matters. It's a small deployment — snacks and souvenirs to smart lockers — but it's a symbolic first for a region that hasn't had drone delivery infrastructure before. Watch whether Alatau can scale past a games-event novelty into something with actual commercial logistics behind it.

Read at Qazinform →

HoverAir Unveils Versa, a Pocket Camera That Transforms Into a Drone

HoverAir

HoverAir has released Versa, a foldable pocket camera drone that unfolds into a flying rig.

Why it matters. A pocket camera that unfolds into a drone is a neat consumer-hardware trick, not a strategic shift, but it shows how fast drone miniaturization is trickling down into everyday gadgets. It's the kind of product that makes aerial filming as casual as a phone photo, quietly widening who gets to fly.

Read at Imaging Resource →

FedEx and Dexterity Expand Physical AI Deployment for Autonomous Trailer Loading at Hagerstown Hub

Dexterity, FedEx

FedEx and Dexterity are expanding their robotic trailer-loading operation from a pilot site to full production scale at the Hagerstown Hub, deploying Dexterity's Foresight world model to handle a task that has resisted automation.

Why it matters. Trailer loading has resisted automation for years because it demands improvisation with irregular packages in tight, shifting spaces — exactly the kind of task world models like Dexterity's Foresight are built for. Moving from pilot to full production at a real FedEx hub is the proof point warehouse robotics vendors have struggled to produce: physical AI doing dirty, unglamorous logistics work at scale.

Read at Dexterity →

Waymo's self-driving cars are helping Austin find potholes. Here's how the pilot is working.

Waymo

Waymo is deploying its autonomous vehicles as mobile sensors to detect road damage for Austin's public works department.

Why it matters. Turning a robotaxi fleet into a rolling infrastructure sensor is a clever second use for hardware that's already driving every street in a city anyway. It's a small pilot, but it points toward a business model where Waymo sells data and civic services, not just rides, to the cities that host it.

Read at kvue.com →

item.title: The Weekly — 2026-W30
item.description: Mitsubishi Motors' entry into mass-producing humanoid robots, Figure AI's pivot toward military hardware on AMD silicon, and AgiBot's Hong Kong IPO filing mark a week where humanoid robotics stopped being a lab curiosity and started looking like an industrial and geopolitical bet.
item.content:encoded:
Mitsubishi Motors' entry into mass-producing humanoid robots, Figure AI's pivot toward military hardware on AMD silicon, and AgiBot's Hong Kong IPO filing mark a week where humanoid robotics stopped being a lab curiosity and started looking like an industrial and geopolitical bet.

This week the humanoid robot graduated from demo reel to balance sheet: a legacy automaker committed to mass production, a Pentagon-adjacent startup lined up new chips, and a Chinese robot maker queued up for public markets. Meanwhile the machines kept finding odder jobs — steering warships, threading catheters, teaching third grade — while regulators in Beijing quietly reopened the robotaxi spigot.

New Humanoid Robot with ‘Smart Skin’ (I Touched It)

Generative Bionics

Generative Bionics unveiled Gene.01, a humanoid robot embedded with touch and proximity sensors that light up when touched, at AMD's Advancing AI conference.

Read at CNET →

M'bishi Motors teams up with startup to mass produce humanoid robots

M'bishi Motors

M'bishi Motors is partnering with a startup to begin mass production of humanoid robots, marking a major automaker's push into physical AI manufacturing.

Why it matters. When a car company with decades of manufacturing scale commits to mass-producing humanoids, it signals the sector has moved past prototype theater into industrial planning. Watch whether Mitsubishi treats this as a side bet or restructures factory lines around it, and whether other automakers follow suit.

Read at Japan Wire by Kyodo News →

New York school district to deploy humanoid robot teacher this fall

Salamanca City Central School District, Realbotix, Andrew Kiguel, Steve Wozniak

A rural New York school district on a Seneca reservation will deploy a humanoid robot named Sally in high school classrooms this fall, partnering with Toronto robotics firm Realbotix.

Read at WKRN News 2 →

Eric Trump-backed Foundation partners with AMD to develop humanoid robots

AMD, Eric Trump Foundation, Eric Trump

An Eric Trump-backed foundation has partnered with AMD to develop humanoid robots, signaling corporate-backed interest in physical AI infrastructure.

Read at Reuters →

Tesla Robotaxi service now goes to SFO

Tesla

Tesla expanded its Robotaxi service to San Francisco International Airport, widening the geographic footprint of its autonomous ride-hailing offering.

Read at KRON4 →

Autonomous drone delivery startup Manna plots major US expansion

Manna

Manna, an autonomous drone delivery startup, is expanding operations across the United States.

Read at TechCrunch →

Introducing KinetIQ

Humanoid

Humanoid has launched KinetIQ, an AI framework for coordinating fleets of robots with different body types across warehouses, stores, and homes using a layered agentic architecture.

Read at Humanoid →

Elevating Healthcare Logistics: Wing Partners with Apian and the NHS for South West London Drone Deliveries

Wing, Apian, South West London Pathology, Simon Brewer

Wing deployed its autonomous drones to ferry blood samples between London hospitals in five minutes, slashing a forty-minute ground journey and moving medical logistics into the air.

Read at Wing →

Wing and Walmart name seven new markets for drone delivery service

Wing, Walmart, Heather Rivera

Wing and Walmart are expanding their drone delivery network to seven new major metros, including Philadelphia and Phoenix, bringing their combined footprint to nearly 20 U.S. markets as they push toward a coast-to-coast reach of 40 million Americans by 2027.

Read at Wing →

South Korean Navy tests humanoid robot as ship helmsman

Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Shim Hyun-chul, Kim Hyung-jun

The South Korean Navy tested Pibot, a humanoid robot developed by KAIST, as a ship's helmsman, following voice commands and operating controls in a simulator.

Read at upi.com →

Tesla expands driverless taxi service in Orlando as autonomous vehicle competition grows

Tesla

Tesla has expanded its driverless taxi service to Orlando, marking another step in its effort to establish a robotaxi footprint amid intensifying competition.

Why it matters. Orlando joins Tesla's growing patchwork of robotaxi cities, each one a data point in whether Musk's camera-only approach can scale against Waymo's sensor-heavy fleets. The real test isn't launch headlines but incident rates once the novelty wears off.

Read at FOX 35 Orlando →

Anduril Thunder Autonomous Attack Rotorcraft Is a Flying Arsenal of Strike Munitions

Anduril

Anduril's Thunder is an autonomous attack helicopter designed to carry and deploy strike munitions without a pilot.

Read at autoevolution →

Humanoid Brings Voice-Activated Multi-Robot Collaboration Powered by KinetIQ to Life at NVIDIA GTC

Humanoid, NVIDIA

Humanoid demonstrated its KinetIQ fleet-management system at NVIDIA GTC, orchestrating multiple robots to interpret voice commands and coordinate physical tasks in real time.

Why it matters. Coordinating a fleet of robots via voice command is a software problem as much as a hardware one, and NVIDIA's stage presence suggests it wants to own the orchestration layer the way it owns GPUs. Fleet-management middleware could end up being the more durable business than any single robot body.

Read at Humanoid →

Wing's homecoming: Bringing drone delivery to the Bay Area

Wing, Google, Walmart, DoorDash

Wing, Google's drone-delivery subsidiary, is expanding its service to the San Francisco Bay Area after completing over 750,000 residential deliveries across other major U.S. cities.

Why it matters. Wing choosing the Bay Area for its next market, after 750,000 deliveries elsewhere, is a bet on dense, tech-tolerant suburbs as the proving ground for drone logistics at scale. Google's continued investment here matters for how seriously Alphabet still takes hardware moonshots.

Read at Wing →

Wayve, Uber and Nissan Announce Collaboration on Robotaxis

Wayve, Uber, Nissan

Wayve, the London autonomous-driving startup, will supply its AI driving system to Uber and Nissan for robotaxi deployment.

Read at Wayve →

Chinese robot maker AgiBot starts Hong Kong IPO process, Securities Times reports

AgiBot

AgiBot, a Chinese humanoid-robot maker, has begun the process of listing on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Why it matters. A humanoid robot maker heading to public markets is a test of whether investors believe the category has revenue, not just demos. AgiBot's valuation on debut will set a benchmark that Figure, Unitree, and others will be measured against.

Read at Reuters →

Samsung Launches Humanoid Robot Division With Robot-Brain AI Already Tested in Factories

Samsung

Samsung has launched a dedicated humanoid robot division with AI trained on factory floor experience.

Read at Tech Times →

Fellows Participate in First Teleoperated Humanoid Robot Surgery

University of California, San Diego, Garth R. Jacobsen, Ryan Broderick

Surgeons at UC San Diego used teleoperated humanoid robots to perform gallbladder removal, suggesting cheaper robotic surgery for rural and resource-limited hospitals.

Why it matters. Teleoperated humanoids performing gallbladder surgery is aimed squarely at rural hospitals that can't afford a Da Vinci system or a surgeon on call. If the cost math works, this could democratize robotic surgery faster than any incremental improvement to existing platforms.

Read at The American College of Surgeons →

item.title: The Weekly — 2026-W29
item.description: Figure unveiled its third-generation humanoid, Figure 03, alongside a Helix upgrade that lets robots learn new chores straight from video; NEURA Robotics struck a major chip-and-software alliance with Qualcomm to standardize humanoid 'brains'; and Anduril's autonomous drone fired its first live missile, quietly formalizing a new class of lethal, uncrewed weapons.
item.content:encoded:
Figure unveiled its third-generation humanoid, Figure 03, alongside a Helix upgrade that lets robots learn new chores straight from video; NEURA Robotics struck a major chip-and-software alliance with Qualcomm to standardize humanoid 'brains'; and Anduril's autonomous drone fired its first live missile, quietly formalizing a new class of lethal, uncrewed weapons.

This week the humanoid race shifted from demo-day flourish to something closer to infrastructure. Figure, NEURA Robotics, and Dexterity all made moves toward robots that generalize and scale, while GeniusRobotics claimed a manufacturing first and Anduril's missile test reminded everyone that autonomy's hardest edges are still military ones.

'World's 1st mass-produced humanoid robot' motors to market in China

GeniusRobotics

GeniusRobotics' Ares humanoid robot enters mass production in China, marking the first commercially scaled humanoid platform.

Why it matters. GeniusRobotics claims a manufacturing first that Tesla, Figure, and Unitree have all chased but not yet publicly claimed. The real test isn't the announcement but unit economics and reliability at scale — mass production means nothing if the robots can't hold up outside a showroom.

Read at New Atlas →

New York school district to deploy humanoid robot in classrooms this fall

Realbotix

Realbotix is deploying humanoid robots into New York school district classrooms this fall to teach STEM subjects.

Why it matters. A public school district putting humanoid robots in front of children is a real-world trust test that no lab demo can substitute for. Watch how Realbotix handles safety oversight and whether teachers actually find the robots useful, or just distracting.

Read at Fox News →

ACE ROBOTICS Unveils Kairos 3.1 and Expands Its Embodied AI Stack from Data to Deployment at WAIC 2026

ACE Robotics

ACE Robotics unveiled Kairos 3.1, an embodied AI system spanning data collection to robot deployment, at WAIC 2026.

Why it matters. ACE Robotics is building a full-stack embodied AI system — data to deployment — that mirrors what Physical Intelligence and Figure are attempting in the US. It's another signal that China's robotics ecosystem is racing to own the entire pipeline, not just the hardware.

Read at Yahoo Finance →

Chinese platform lets people control humanoid robots with thoughts

BrainCo

BrainCo unveiled a brain-computer interface platform that lets users control humanoid robots directly with their thoughts via EEG headsets.

Why it matters. BrainCo's brain-computer interface layer for humanoid control points toward teleoperation that skips joysticks and controllers entirely. It's early and gimmicky-looking now, but latency and accuracy improvements here could matter for hazardous or remote work down the line.

Read at Interesting Engineering →

Humanoid robot lands head-high kick during ‘world’s first freestyle’ fighting in China

EngineAI

EngineAI's T800 humanoid robot landed a head-high kick at China's first freestyle robot fighting tournament.

Why it matters. EngineAI's fighting robot is pure spectacle, but the durability flex — a headless robot still swinging — is a marketing tactic other humanoid makers will feel pressure to match. Expect more staged combat as firms compete for viral proof of ruggedness.

Read at Interesting Engineering →

Tesla's Robotaxi Just Launched in Miami. Here's How Small the Service Area Really Is

Tesla

Tesla launched its Robotaxi service in Miami with a notably constrained operating territory.

Why it matters. Tesla's robotaxi keeps expanding, but a tiny operating footprint in Miami underscores how far the fleet remains from Waymo-scale coverage. The gap between headline launches and actual usable service area is the real story to track.

Read at Yahoo Finance →

World-first airdrop of an autonomous drone boat into rough seas

Kraken Technologies

The Royal Navy airdropped a Kraken Technologies autonomous drone boat from an RAF cargo plane into rough North Sea waters.

Why it matters. Airdropping an autonomous drone boat from a cargo plane into rough North Sea waters is a real test of rapid-deployment logistics, not a lab exercise. If it works reliably, it changes how navies think about getting unmanned assets into contested waters fast.

Read at New Atlas →

Matternet taps Beeline to accelerate US drone delivery expansion

Matternet, Beeline

Matternet partners with Beeline to scale drone delivery operations across the United States.

Why it matters. Matternet's partnership with Beeline is a quiet infrastructure play to scale drone delivery across the US, competing directly with Wing and Zipline for logistics contracts. Watch how fast regulatory approvals and airspace integration keep pace with expansion ambitions.

Read at DroneDJ →

Anduril Autonomous Drone Fires Its First-Ever Live Missile at a Target

Anduril

Anduril's autonomous drone successfully fired a live missile at a target, marking the company's first weaponized flight test.

Why it matters. Anduril's autonomous drone firing a live missile is the moment lethal autonomy stops being a slide-deck concept and becomes a demonstrated capability. It puts pressure on the Pentagon's procurement pipeline and raises the stakes for how quickly regulators and treaties can catch up.

Read at autoevolution →

A mosquito-hunting killer drone is available for preorder – and I have questions

Tornyol, Alex Toussaint

Tornyol, a Y Combinator-backed startup, is taking preorders for an autonomous micro-drone that hunts mosquitoes by tracking their wingbeat and colliding with them mid-flight.

Why it matters. A consumer preorder for a mosquito-killing drone shows autonomous flight tech diffusing into oddball civilian niches, well beyond delivery and surveillance. The obvious question is whether it can actually target mosquitoes without misfiring on anything else that moves.

Read at TechRadar →

US picks containerized drone system for next-gen autonomous warfare

Tesseract Ventures, Defense Innovation Unit, John Boucard

The Pentagon tapped Kansas City-based Tesseract Ventures to develop containerized drone pods that let one operator manage multiple aircraft with minimal human intervention.

Why it matters. The Pentagon standardizing on containerized drone systems is a bet on modularity — units that can be shipped, deployed, and swapped like cargo. It's infrastructure procurement, less flashy than a missile test but arguably more consequential for how fast autonomous warfare scales.

Read at Interesting Engineering →

Introducing Figure 03

Figure

Figure introduced Figure 03, its third-generation humanoid robot redesigned for manufacturing and trained on proprietary Helix AI.

Why it matters. Figure 03 is a redesign explicitly aimed at manufacturing scale, not lab demos, and it's trained on the company's own Helix AI rather than borrowed foundation models. This puts direct pressure on Tesla's Optimus and Unitree to show comparable production-readiness, not just impressive footage.

Read at Figure →

Helix 02 Living Room Tidy

Figure

Figure's Helix 02 robot tidies living rooms using coordinated tool use and learns new household tasks from video.

Why it matters. A robot that learns new household tasks straight from video, without retraining, is the generalization breakthrough the whole humanoid industry has been chasing. If it holds up outside curated demos, it's a bigger deal than any single hardware upgrade this year.

Read at Figure →

NEURA Robotics and Qualcomm Enter Strategic Collaboration to Advance Physical AI and Cognitive Robotics

NEURA Robotics, Qualcomm

NEURA Robotics and Qualcomm announced a partnership to develop a 'Brain + Nervous System' reference architecture for humanoid robots.

Why it matters. NEURA and Qualcomm's 'Brain + Nervous System' architecture is an attempt to standardize the chips-and-software stack that every humanoid maker currently builds in isolation. If it catches on, it becomes a real challenge to Nvidia's dominance in robotics compute.

Read at Neura Robotics →

Introducing Foresight

Dexterity

Dexterity unveiled Foresight, a world model for robotic manipulation trained on over 100 million real warehouse actions.

Why it matters. Dexterity's Foresight is a world model trained on 100 million real warehouse actions, aimed at letting robots predict physical outcomes rather than just react. It's a direct competitive shot at Physical Intelligence and Covariant in the race to make warehouse robots reason, not just grasp.

Read at Dexterity →

Wing and Papa Johns partner to build the future of fresh, hot delivery by drone

Wing, Papa Johns

Wing and Papa Johns launched a drone-delivery pilot in Charlotte to fly hot pizza to customers via app integration.

Why it matters. Papa Johns betting on drone delivery, integrated into its own AI ordering app, signals fast food is ready to treat drones as a real logistics channel, not a novelty. Charlotte is the pilot; the real story is whether the unit economics survive scaling past one city.

Read at Wing →

Autonomous OGI Drones now Alternative Test Method for EPA Subpart OOOOa, OOOOb

Percepto

Percepto's autonomous drone system won EPA approval as an alternative method for methane leak detection at oil and gas sites.

Why it matters. EPA approval for Percepto's autonomous methane-detection drones is a rare regulatory win that could replace manual inspection crews across oil and gas sites. It's a quiet but concrete example of autonomy actually being adopted for environmental compliance, not just demoed.

Read at Percepto →

International Association of Campus Law Enforcement Administrators Launches National Campus Drone Readiness Program, Selecting Draganfly to Provide Drone Systems, Services and Training in Alignment with Emerging U.S. Drone Policy

Draganfly

Draganfly secured a contract to equip campus police departments nationwide with drones and training through a new program.

Read at Draganfly →

item.title: The Weekly — 2026-W28
item.description: 1X gave its Neo humanoid near-human hands and Mitsubishi joined the android race with a 2027 factory plan, while Waymo pushed driverless rides into a half-dozen new cities and Ondas snapped up drone maker DZYNE for $875.8 million.
item.content:encoded:
1X gave its Neo humanoid near-human hands and Mitsubishi joined the android race with a 2027 factory plan, while Waymo pushed driverless rides into a half-dozen new cities and Ondas snapped up drone maker DZYNE for $875.8 million.

The humanoids arrived in force this week, some promising companionship and others promising to replace factory shifts, though nearly every founder spent as much energy managing expectations as raising them. Meanwhile the machines that already work for a living—Waymo's robotaxis and a fleet of autonomous drones from Everest to Tampa Bay—quietly expanded, a reminder that the future often shows up as logistics rather than spectacle.

Humanoid robot designed ‘for a lifetime’ of companionship unveiled

UBTech

UBTech unveiled the U1, a mass-production humanoid robot with emotional AI designed for lifelong companionship.

Why it matters. Another entrant stakes its claim on the emotional-companion niche, a category more marketed than proven. The gap between a demo that charms and a machine someone loves for years remains vast, and this launch does little to close it.

Read at The Independent →

Human-Level Hands? 1X Just Gave Humanoid Robot Neo Something Close

1X

1X upgraded its Neo humanoid robot with more dexterous hands for human-level precision and touch sensitivity.

Why it matters. Hands are the hardest part of the humanoid problem, and dexterity is where the vaporware gets separated from the useful. If Neo's new fingers can genuinely fold laundry or handle fragile objects, 1X inches the whole field closer to homes rather than stages.

Read at Forbes →

The first commercial human-like robot is here. Are replicants next?

A startup shipped its first humanoid robot to customers, raising questions about machines becoming servants or competitors.

Why it matters. Shipping a humanoid to paying customers, even a handful, marks the shift from lab curiosity to commercial product. The philosophical hand-wringing about servants versus rivals matters less than the mundane question of what the thing can actually do once it's unboxed.

Read at Fast Company →

This humanoid robotics company is going public, but its CEO isn't promising a robot in your home anytime soon

Agility Robotics, Peggy Johnson

Agility Robotics, led by Peggy Johnson, is going public via SPAC merger, becoming the first pure-play humanoid robotics company to trade publicly.

Why it matters. A humanoid company reaching public markets while its own CEO tamps down the home-robot fantasy is a rare moment of candor in a hype-drunk sector. Public investors will now get to price the distance between the promise and the shipping manifest.

Read at TechCrunch →

Mitsubishi joins global robot race, plans to manufacture, deploy humanoid workers in 2027

Mitsubishi

Mitsubishi enters the humanoid robotics race with plans to manufacture and deploy robotic workers by 2027.

Why it matters. When a $200 billion industrial conglomerate commits to building and deploying humanoids, the field gains manufacturing muscle the startups lack. Mitsubishi's 2027 target puts it in direct competition with Tesla and the venture-funded pack, and factory floors are where these robots have the clearest business case.

Read at Automotive News →

Ex-Tesla Optimus scientist unveils European humanoid robot startup

UMA, Tesla, Hugging Face, Figure, BMW, Boston Dynamics, Hyundai, Greycroft, Relentless, Unity Growth, Datadog, DeepMind, Nvidia, Rémi Cadène, Simon Alibert, Rob Knight, Yann LeCun, Olivier Pomel, Thomas Wolf, Elon Musk

Rémi Cadène, who led AI systems at Tesla's Optimus lab, is launching UMA, a Paris-based humanoid robot startup targeting Europe's aging workforce and industrial warehouses.

Why it matters. The Optimus diaspora continues, with Tesla alumni seeding rival ventures the way PayPal's did a generation ago. A European base is a bet that the continent's factories want a homegrown alternative rather than an American or Chinese one.

Read at Electrek →

Waymo launching robotaxi service in Denver. But only for its own workers.

Waymo

Waymo is quietly testing its Denver robotaxi service on employees before facing actual customers.

Why it matters. Testing on employees lets Waymo gather Denver's altitude-and-snow data without exposing paying riders to the learning curve. It's the cautious playbook that has let the company outlast flashier rivals; the tell will be how quickly the captive audience gives way to the public.

Read at The Colorado Sun →

Waymo to start driverless rides in 4 more U.S. markets as expansion accelerates

Waymo

Waymo is pushing into four new cities as the company turns its longest-running robotaxi experiment into something resembling a real business.

Why it matters. Four new markets at once signals Waymo has moved from proving the concept to scaling it, the phase where unit economics finally get scrutinized. Every city added widens the moat against Cruise's wreckage and Tesla's still-unproven robotaxi promises.

Read at CNBC →

Waymo's vehicles ready to drive themselves in San Diego, company says

Waymo

Waymo is expanding its autonomous taxi service to San Diego, another notch in its methodical march toward mainstream driverless operations.

Why it matters. San Diego joins the roster as Waymo methodically stitches together a national footprint one metro at a time. The consistency is the story: no grand announcements, just a widening map that competitors now have to catch.

Read at NBC 7 San Diego →

Waymo comes to Tampa — who is responsible?

Waymo

Waymo's arrival in Tampa raises immediate questions about liability when self-driving cars inevitably collide with the city's notoriously aggressive drivers.

Why it matters. Tampa's arrival surfaces the liability question that shadows every driverless deployment: when a robot and a human trade paint, whose insurer pays? These are the unglamorous legal precedents that will shape the industry as much as any software update.

Read at FOX 13 Tampa Bay →

BayCare Selects Zipline to Build Drone Delivery Network Across Tampa Bay

BayCare, Zipline

BayCare, Florida's largest health system, taps Zipline to deploy autonomous drones for moving blood and medical supplies across Tampa Bay.

Why it matters. Blood and medical supplies are drone delivery's genuine killer app, where minutes matter and roads don't. BayCare's endorsement gives Zipline a marquee health-system deployment and a template other hospital networks will study.

Read at Dronelife →

ZenaTech begins development of sphere-shaped autonomous drone

ZenaTech

ZenaTech is building a spherical autonomous drone, betting rounded geometry solves problems rectangular designs don't.

Why it matters. A spherical drone is either a clever answer to durability and safety in tight spaces or a novelty in search of a use case. ZenaTech is wagering that shape is a differentiator; the market will decide whether geometry is a feature or a gimmick.

Read at Investing.com →

Skydio crosses 1,000 drone Dock deployments in just one year

Skydio

Skydio's autonomous charging dock reached 1,000 deployments in one year, validating the company's unattended flight strategy.

Why it matters. The dock, not the drone, is the quiet breakthrough: it turns a piloted gadget into an unattended sentry that recharges itself. A thousand deployments in a year suggests the autonomous-inspection market is maturing from pilot projects into standing infrastructure.

Read at DroneDJ →

Beyond the Helicopter: DJI’s EV50 drone brings autonomous logistics to the slopes of Mount Everest

DJI

DJI's heavy-lift EV50 drone is being tested to ferry supplies up Everest's slopes, stress-testing autonomous mountain logistics.

Why it matters. Hauling gear up Everest is equal parts marketing and genuine engineering trial, thin air and brutal cold being unforgiving referees. If DJI's heavy-lift drone survives the mountain, the more mundane payoff is autonomous logistics for mines, farms, and construction sites everywhere else.

Read at sUAS News →

Percepto Unveils AI-Powered Inspection Intelligence Platform for Energy Infrastructure and Autonomous Drone Operations

Percepto

Percepto launches an AI-powered inspection platform enabling drones to autonomously monitor power grids without human pilots.

Why it matters. The value in drone inspection is migrating from the flying to the interpreting, and Percepto is planting its flag on the analysis layer. For utilities managing aging grids, software that flags a failing transformer before it burns is worth more than the aircraft that photographs it.

Read at uasweekly.com →

Pentagon awards $80M task order for AI-enabled tech to defend Air Force bases against small drones

AeroVironment

AeroVironment wins an $80.5 million task order to deploy AI-powered drone-detection systems at Air Force bases.

Why it matters. The $80 million counter-drone order is the flip side of the cheap-drone revolution: every advance in unmanned attack invites an equal spend on defense. Air Force bases are learning what Ukraine's battlefields already proved, that a $500 quadcopter can threaten billion-dollar assets.

Read at DefenseScoop →

Ondas to Buy Military Drone Maker DZYNE for $875.8 Million

Ondas, DZYNE

Ondas is acquiring military drone maker DZYNE for $875.8 million to expand its defense sector presence.

Why it matters. At nearly $876 million, this acquisition is the week's biggest check and a bet that defense budgets will keep favoring unmanned systems. Consolidation is coming to the military drone sector, and Ondas is positioning to be a buyer rather than a target.

Read at Bloomberg.com →

Develop Humanoid Robot Policies End-to-End with NVIDIA Isaac GR00T | NVIDIA Technical Blog

NVIDIA

NVIDIA's Isaac GR00T software pipeline enables training humanoid robots for complex physical tasks without simulation code.

Why it matters. By handing developers a ready-made pipeline for training humanoid behaviors, NVIDIA cements its position as the picks-and-shovels supplier to the entire robot rush. Every startup that builds on GR00T deepens dependence on NVIDIA's stack, the same playbook that made the company indispensable to generative AI.

Read at NVIDIA Developer →
